title: Gemini Notebook: A Source-Checked Workflow for Comparing Software Quotes
body_md: **Quick answer:** Gemini Notebook, previously called NotebookLM, is worth trying when you need to answer a question from a small set of documents. Start with the free Standard tier, but do not confuse source-grounded answers with guaranteed accuracy or permanent free access. ## What changed, and what did not Google announced the rename to Gemini Notebook on 16 July 2026, with a rollout to personal and Workspace accounts over several weeks. It is the same standalone product, with deeper Google integration and a secure cloud computer that can run code. A familiar NotebookLM name in an older guide does not mean it describes a different product. The official plan page still offers Standard free of charge, and the higher tiers are not sold separately — they ride along with Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra subscriptions. Limits, feature access and availability can change. This is not a promise of $0 forever, and paid plans should be checked for both features and usage limits before you buy. ## A practical use case: compare two software proposals Imagine a freelancer choosing a project-management service. One vendor quotes per user, another per workspace; annual discounts make the monthly headline misleading. Rather than ask a chatbot which product is best, use the proposals to find the missing information. 1. **Check permission before uploading.** Use public proposals or documents you are authorised to share. Do not upload a client contract, employee data or credentials just because the tool is free. Check your organisation's requirements and the terms for the account you use. 2. **Create a narrowly scoped notebook.** Name it for one decision, not your entire business. Add the two current proposals and, if permitted, your own requirements note. 3. **Label the sources.** Include vendor, document date, currency and billing period in your notes. A dollar figure from a US page is not a UK pound price. Check tax treatment in the quote rather than assuming VAT or sales tax is included. 4. **Ask for facts, gaps and citations separately.** Tell the notebook not to fill missing fields from general knowledge. 5. **Open each cited passage.** Confirm the price basis, minimum seats, cancellation terms and renewal conditions yourself. A citation can point to text that does not support the whole answer. 6. **Ask the vendor about gaps.** If the source does not state an export fee, write "not stated," not "free." Keep the original documents outside the notebook. ### A prompt you can adapt > Using only the selected proposals, compare Vendor A and Vendor B for five users over 12 months. For each item, identify the source: billing currency, monthly versus annual commitment, minimum seats, tax treatment, cancellation terms and data export. Write "not stated" when a proposal does not specify something. Separate facts from assumptions. Do not convert currencies or recommend a winner until the missing terms are resolved. This is a suggested workflow, not a claim that the product will execute every instruction correctly. The human review is part of the process. ## Do the annual-cost arithmetic outside the summary Suppose a hypothetical offer is £12 per user per month with annual billing and a five-seat minimum. The annual subscription would be £12 × 5 × 12 = £720 before any additional tax or charges. An introductory three-month discount cannot be treated as a permanent rate. If another proposal is in US dollars, compare the contractual terms first and make any currency conversion explicitly dated. That calculation adds more decision value than a broad "best app" ranking. It is deliberately an example, not a current vendor price. ## Source-grounded does not mean the whole product is source-only Google's help documentation describes chat responses based on source data with citations. It also describes uses with or without sources and additional capabilities such as web research. Be clear about which mode and sources you are using. For an evidence-based memo, stick to the selected material, verify the citations and preserve unresolved questions. Neither a source-grounded notebook nor a general chatbot should be treated as a substitute for reading the decisive contract clause. Before the memo goes out, check that every important factual claim has a source you opened, that missing details are labelled rather than guessed, that currencies and billing periods are explicit, that your recommendation is separate from the vendors' claims, and that the original documents remain accessible independently of the AI tool. ## Why usage can run out before you expect Google's usage-limit guidance describes compute-based limits that took effect on 2 September 2026, factoring in prompt complexity, the models and features used and the length of your chat, with the quota refreshing every five hours up to a weekly limit. Workload matters, not just the number of questions. The old fixed daily counts a review may quote — 50 chats and three Audio Overviews a day on the free tier, for instance — are no longer how the free plan is metered. Storage caps are separate and still fixed by plan. Standard allows 100 notebooks, 50 sources per notebook and 500,000 words per source, which is more than a two-proposal comparison will ever need. ## When paying makes sense Try a small, representative project first. Record what blocks you: the number of sources, a feature you need, or repeated usage limits. Then compare the official plans available for your account and country. Google AI Plus gets twice the standard allowance and Google AI Pro four times, with Ultra at 5x or 20x Pro — priced in the US at $4.99, $19.99 and $99.99 or $199.99 a month at the time of writing. If you only need one short document summarised occasionally, a new paid subscription may add little. If you cannot upload the material under your organisation's policy, a higher tier does not automatically solve that permission problem. **Correction note:** This revision removes the unsupported "$0 forever" promise and the claim that paid plans only increase volume. It also narrows the earlier source-only claim to source-grounded chat and replaces unverified pricing assertions with an auditable worked example. *Updated October 2026. This guide is based on Google's published documentation and public reports, not a hands-on test; the vendor figures are hypothetical and use no confidential material.* ## My Take My read is that the rename is the least interesting thing here and the September metering change is the most interesting. A fixed "50 chats a day" was something you could plan around. A compute budget that refreshes every five hours and depends on how hard your prompt is cannot be planned around, which means the free tier is now great for a one-afternoon document comparison and unreliable for anything you have to deliver on a deadline. I think the quote-comparison job is close to the best use of this tool, precisely because it is small. Two PDFs, six fields, every answer checkable in one click. The failure mode of general chatbots on procurement questions is confident invention of a renewal term, and a citation you can open is a real defence against that — not a perfect one, since a citation can point at text that does not actually support the sentence built on it. The fair point against me: for a lot of people the free tier never runs out, and paying $19.99 a month for Pro only to compare two vendor quotes would be silly. The free allowance is genuinely generous for one person. If the limits bite, the upgrade is also not a standalone purchase — you are buying a whole Google AI plan, which is only worth it if you want the rest of it. What I would watch is whether Google keeps folding Notebook features into the broader Gemini app. The value of a notebook is that it refuses to answer from the open web. Every integration that blurs that line makes the tool slightly less trustworthy for exactly the job described above, so check which mode you are in before you quote a number back to a vendor. I am not a lawyer or an accountant, and nothing above is legal or financial advice. For a contract you are actually signing, the clause in the document beats any summary of it, including one with footnotes.
